question.title: Symptom-Based vs Cause-Based Alerting: Avoiding High CPU Pages
question.scenario: A junior engineer sets up an alert in Opsgenie: 'Page on-call if any Kubernetes pod reaches 85% CPU utilization for 3 minutes'. The on-call engineer gets woken up at 3:00 AM, but customers report zero degradation, APIs are responding in 15ms, and the pod was simply running a scheduled background batch task cleanly within limits.
question.question: Why is alerting directly on high CPU or memory considered an anti-pattern ('cause-based alerting'), and what should on-call paging alerts be based on instead ('symptom-based alerting')?
hints: Customers do not care if your CPU is at 90% as long as their checkout API returns 200 OK within 100ms.
Cause-based alerts create noise; symptom-based alerts protect the customer experience.
question.answer:
1. Cause-Based Alerting: Alerts triggered on underlying symptoms or resource utilization (e.g., CPU > 85%, memory > 80%, disk I/O spike). Pitfall: High CPU is often intentional (efficient hardware utilization or batch tasks). Alerting on it wakes engineers up when user-facing service is completely healthy, causing alert fatigue.

2. Symptom-Based Alerting (User-Facing / SLO Alerts): Alerts triggered when customers are actually experiencing pain (e.g., HTTP 5xx error rate exceeds 1% of total requests, or p95 API latency exceeds 500ms). 

Best Practice:
- PagerDuty/Opsgenie pages (wake humans up) should strictly be Symptom-Based (SLO burn rate, customer-impacting failures).
- High CPU / memory alerts should be Cause-Based tickets or dashboard warnings (non-urgent, investigating capacity during office hours).
question.pitfalls: Paging on-call engineers for high CPU, memory, or garbage collection pauses when user-facing error rates and latencies are completely unaffected; neglecting to link runbooks to alerts.
question.key_takeaway: Page humans on symptoms that hurt customers (high error rate, tail latency). Route causes (high CPU, disk usage trends) to dashboards or ticket queues.
